title: Phase 1 · Stage 1: A catalog card
summary: Meet Shelfwise, the library system you will build in 32 stages, and print its first catalog card.

steps.title: Welcome to Shelfwise
body: This is the capstone of the C# track. Over **32 stages in 10 phases** you will build **Shelfwise**, the system a small public library runs on: a catalog of books, members with different memberships, loans with due dates, fines, reports, files, background reminders and finally a web API with authentication.

It is one program that grows. Every stage starts from **your own code** from the stage before, so by the end you will have written every line of a real application, most of them several times. That repetition is the point: the goal is that you could start a fresh `Program.cs` tomorrow and build something like it from memory.
| Phase | You add |
| 1 Foundations | variables, a command loop, methods, collections |
| 2 Modelling | classes, records, enums, inheritance, value objects |
| 3 Robustness | nullability, exceptions, a `Result<T>`, pattern matching |
| 4 Collections & LINQ | repositories, queries, reports, extension methods |
| 5 Generics & delegates | a generic repository, filter pipelines, domain events |
| 6 Files | JSON snapshots, a versioned format, CSV import and export |
| 7 Async | async storage, `Task.WhenAll`, cancellation, reminders |
| 8 Architecture | layers, a clock and ids you can control, dependency injection |
| 9 Web API | minimal APIs, DTOs, ProblemDetails, paging, middleware, auth |
| 10 Quality | your own tests, SOLID refactoring, shipping it |
Every stage lists **Learn it first** lessons above its steps. If a stage feels hard, open one: you come straight back to the step you were on.
Stage 1 is small on purpose: hold the facts about one book in variables and print them as a catalog card.
```csharp
string title = "The Hobbit";
int year = 1937;
decimal finePerDay = 0.50m;
Console.WriteLine($"{title} ({year})");        // The Hobbit (1937)
Console.WriteLine($"Fine: {finePerDay:C}");    // Fine: $0.50

steps.prompt: Each fact about a book needs a type. Match each value to the type that should hold it.
steps.explain: An ISBN looks like a number but you never do arithmetic on it, and it has dashes (and sometimes an X), so it is text. Money is always `decimal`; `double` cannot store 0.10 exactly.

steps.prompt: Interpolated strings can format as they print. What does this print? (The dojo runs with the en-US culture.)
steps.explain: `:C` formats as currency. After a comma comes a **width**: positive pads on the left (right-aligned), negative pads on the right (left-aligned). Both are handy for tables.

steps.prompt: Complete the line so it prints `The Hobbit by J.R.R. Tolkien (1937)`.
steps.explain: The `$` turns on interpolation; each `{...}` holds an expression.

steps.title: The first catalog card
prompt: Create the variables for one book and print its catalog card.
Print exactly, using interpolated strings and `:C` for the fine:
starter: // Declare the variables from the table, then print the catalog card.

require.message: Stores the fine in a decimal called finePerDay
Stores the year in an int

hints: One line per variable: `type name = value;`. A `decimal` literal needs the `m` suffix: `0.50m`.
Print with `Console.WriteLine($"...")` and put each variable inside `{ }`.
The last line is `Console.WriteLine($"Fine per day: {finePerDay:C}");`.

steps.title: Reading the book from input
body: A card that only ever shows *The Hobbit* is not much use. Real data arrives as **text**: from a keyboard, a file, or here, the test's input. `Console.ReadLine()` reads one line and returns `string?`: a string, or `null` when the input has run out.
```csharp
string title = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";             // "" if there was no line
int year = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine() ?? "0");     // text -> number
const int CurrentYear = 2026;
Console.WriteLine($"Age: {CurrentYear - year} years");
- `??` says *use the right side when the left is null*. Phase 3 is all about null; for now it keeps the compiler happy.
- `int.Parse` turns `"1937"` into the number `1937` so you can do arithmetic. (Stage 2 handles input that is not a number.)
- `const` is a value fixed at compile time. Shelfwise pretends it is always **2026** so that every run prints the same thing.
A fixed-width row lines columns up: `$"|{title,-24}|{year,5}|"` pads the title to 24 characters on the right and the year to 5 on the left.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program reads a year and prints how old the book is.
steps.explain: Each line uses something the line above produced, except the constant, which must come before the subtraction that uses it.

steps.title: Read the book from input
prompt: Keep `library`, `version` and `finePerDay` as they are. Instead of fixed values, read the book from five lines of input, in this order: **isbn, title, author, year, copies**.
Then print the card as before, with two additions:
- after `Copies:` an `Age:` line: `2026` minus the year (use a `const int CurrentYear = 2026;`),

- a last line with the book as a fixed-width row: `|`, the title padded to **24** characters (left-aligned), `|`, the author padded to **18** (left-aligned), `|`, the year in **5** (right-aligned), `|`, the copies in **3** (right-aligned), `|`.
Every input in this stage is well formed.

tests.name: a newer book with one copy

hints: Five `Console.ReadLine()` calls, one per line of input, in the order isbn, title, author, year, copies.
Numbers need converting: `int year = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine() ?? "0");`. The age is `CurrentYear - year`.
